topic: a packing-slip generator that renders fixed-width slips from an orders CSV with strict rules for grouping, quantities, weights, address blocks, page breaks and totals
calibration:
Calibration: recent tasks under these rules and how often the reference agent solved them (target: 1-3 of 5 runs).
Per kind: judgement/property_completeness: 2 task(s), 3/5, 3/5
- http-header-crlf-injection-audit [property_completeness]: 3/5 -> learnable (The task split 3/2 pass/fail because of a critical ambiguity: the instructions didn't clearly specify that CRLF must be stripped/sanitized rather than rejected with 400 errors, so one failing agent rejected requests entirely (breaking test_redirect_no_crlf, test_request_id_no_crlf) while another's sanitization crashed the server (breaking test_clean_redirect_still_works and others). All passing runs correctly stripped CRLF while preserving normal HTTP functionality across redirect, cookie, request-id, and display-name paths. Next design should add an explicit rule distinguishing 'sanitize by stripping' from 'reject with error' and keep the dual-property structure (security + functionality) since the mutation check killed all 5 faults.). Fix all CRLF injection vulnerabilities across a small URL-shortener HTTP service that sets headers through varied code paths and abstraction layers.
- billing-rounding-consistency [property_completeness]: 3/5 -> too_easy (The billing-rounding-consistency task was well-tested (all 11 mutations killed) but too easy for agents, who passed in only 8–10 steps; the 'invalid' outcomes were environment issues rather than difficulty. The next design should keep the strong mutation-killing test coverage but add more independent rules around new billing edge cases (e.g., currency conversion rounding, tax-tier boundaries, multi-item discount interactions) to increase task depth and require more than a quick fix.). Fix a billing module where several code paths round monetary amounts using different methods, violating the round-half-up business rule.
Tasks solved too often had few rules, rules on one theme, or an oracle to compare against. Make this design harder with more independent, precisely stated rules on more themes and sharper hidden inputs; never by hiding rules. Make it easier than the too_hard ones.

too_easy_because: R5 has mathematically incorrect test values: 0.1225 does not round to 0.124 under any method (round-half-up gives 0.123, banker's gives 0.122). An agent implementing round-half-up correctly would produce 0.123 and fail a test expecting 0.124. This is unfair.

R1 and R8 are ambiguous about whether '72 characters' means Unicode codepoints or visual columns. For lines with CJK, these interpretations produce different outputs. The test plan says '73 bytes' which is wrong for non-ASCII lines (U+2550 is 3 bytes in UTF-8).
R5 is ambiguous about whether 'item weight' means unit_weight from the CSV or quantity×unit_weight. Two reasonable readings produce different item line weights and different totals.

R14 is vague: 'description-positioned line' does not specify exact columns; '...and N more items' vs '... and N more items' (space after dots) is inconsistent between instruction_summary and requirements.

R15 is ambiguous: 'value matches YYYY-MM-DD' could mean regex format match or valid calendar date. '2024-13-45' matches the format but is not a valid date—two reasonable readings give different outputs.
R16 contradicts itself: rule says 'truncated with ... if >37 chars' but test plan boundary says '40 chars = no truncation, 41 chars = truncated'. These are incompatible.
R8 scope is unclear: rule says 'Name and address fields' but visual width padding is also needed for SKU, description, order_id, and slip numbering to maintain 72-visual-column lines.

Many hidden test inputs are identical to examples in instruction_summary: same SKUs (B-2,A-10,A-1), same dates (2024-01-07), same quantities (-3), same item counts (25, 9), same CJK name (田中太郎), same order_id (A1). Agent can pass by matching examples without understanding.
No rule specifies how total weight is computed: sum of unrounded item weights then round, vs sum of pre-rounded item weights. These give different results at boundaries, and tests may check either.
No rule specifies slip ordering across different order_ids (R4 only covers address ordering within an order_id). Default is CSV order; a test might check lexicographic order.
No rule handles whitespace in CSV fields or negative unit_weights—gaps that tests might check without a stated rule.
Half the rules (8 of 16) are formatting; while diverse, the agent 'gets the formatting theme' and handles most in one pass, reducing difficulty.
